articleSummary: New Ebola outbreak in Kongo-Kinshasa and neighboring countries expands. On 15 May there were 246 cases and 48 deaths; by 23 May authorities reported over 700 suspected or confirmed infections and nearly 180 deaths. WHO representative Anne Ancia cautions the outbreak may not end within two months. Oxford-led clinical trials, funded mainly by WHO, are set to begin testing Remdesivir, an antiviral previously used against other Ebola strains, and MBP 134, a monoclonal antibody therapy by Mapp Biopharmaceutical; MBP 134 has not been officially approved but has emergency-use history and is available for the study. No vaccine currently effective against the Bundibugyo variant; vaccines against the Zaire variant do not prevent Bundibugyo infection. Frontline control relies on case isolation, contact tracing, and public education, a challenge in conflict-affected regions with limited personnel. Genetic analyses suggest current Bundibugyo viruses recently jumped from animals; if confirmed, it would be a zoonosis. Risk of Europe import exists but is deemed low.

articleSummary: An international group of scientists warns that leaks of dangerous viruses from laboratories pose a global pandemic risk. Analyzing seven major laboratory incidents from 1955 to 2019, researchers identify common features: early, unexplained spread without a clear animal source, delays in official disclosures, and outbreaks near facilities handling dangerous pathogens. They estimate such incidents could have caused over 1.1 million infections and more than 700,000 deaths worldwide. The discussion resurfaces amid debates on COVID-19 origins; while the study does not examine COVID-19 directly, some experts note features suggestive of laboratory involvement, though conclusive evidence remains elusive. The study also cites polio outbreaks in California, the 1977 H1N1 episode, the Sverdlovsk anthrax accident, SARS in Asia, and the 2019 Lanzhou brucellosis outbreak. Authors urge stronger international biosafety standards and transparent investigations of suspicious epidemics to mitigate future crises.

articleHeadline: Pakistan on high alert as WHO declares Ebola emergency in Congo, Uganda

articleHeadline: Ebola Outbreak Alert: India Issues Travel Advisory for Congo, Uganda, South Sudan
articleSummary: Ebola outbreak prompts India to issue travel advisory against non-essential travel to Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan as authorities monitor cross-border transmission. Despite the outbreak, India reports no Ebola cases linked to the current outbreak, but officials are boosting preparedness with isolation facilities and heightened surveillance, reflecting lessons from COVID-19. Travellers are advised to maintain hygiene, avoid contact with the sick, and report fever or unexplained weakness after returning from affected countries.

articleHeadline: Computational pipeline boosts broad-spectrum Ebola antibody optimization
articleSummary: Two pan-Ebola antibodies engineered via a closed-loop computational-experimental pipeline co-optimizing framework regions (FR) and complementarity-determining regions (CDR) exhibit broadened neutralization against EBOV, SUDV, and BDBV with increased potency. Led by Wei Yang at the National Institute of Pathogen Biology, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College, the team integrated deep mutational scanning (mCSM-AB/mmCSM-AB), predicted ΔΔG and RSA, and iterative experimental testing. For ADI-15878, the W32G-LC variant neutralized EBOV ~17-fold, BDBV ~7-fold, SUDV ~2-fold and partially restored binding to EBOV GP G528E. For ADI-15946, variants H27Q/S52Y/G66R-LC and A50Y/S52Y/L54R-LC boosted SUDV neutralization >40-fold and >100-fold while retaining EBOV/BDBV activity. Structural/affinity validation (AlphaFold3, SPR) showed expanded interfaces and sub-nanomolar affinities (2.24 nM to ~0.25–0.35 nM). Published in Research (DOI 10.34133/research.1211); prospects include extending to influenza and SARS-CoV-2.

articleSummary: On May 24, 2026, Vietnam's Department of Medical Examination and Treatment urged health facilities and provincial health departments to strengthen Ebola prevention and control, enhance surveillance, and enforce rigorous screening and isolation of suspected or confirmed cases. Transmission occurs via direct contact with tissues, blood, or body fluids of infected humans or animals, and via contaminated equipment. WHO reports from May 5–20 in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda recorded about 600 suspected cases and 139 deaths, with more than 50 laboratory-confirmed infections of Bundibugyo, one of the six Ebola species. articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo intensifies in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri, in a region scarred by armed conflict, insecurity, and massive internal displacement that cripples health services. Poor road networks, seasonal rains, and volatile security corridors delay detection, transport, and quarantining, allowing transmission chains to extend before intervention. Rebellious groups, notably M23, and overlapping local authorities hinder reliable public-health data flows and response coordination. Ituri hosts hundreds of thousands living in crowded camps, raising concerns that a camp-based case could quickly spread due to dense contact networks and mobility. Operationally, rapid case finding, contact tracing, and isolation must be conducted on-site with consistent data collection and decision-maker feedback, but safety risks and disrupted infrastructure fragment these processes. Technical approaches to mobility, data capture, and coordination—such as mobile teams and motorcycle outreach—are viewed as essential to stopping transmission.

articleHeadline: Ebola: What we know about Bundibugyo
articleSummary: As of May 24, 2026, Bundibugyo virus, an Ebola-related pathogen, is driving a Congo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with suspected fatalities exceeding 130. There are no specific treatments or vaccines, and the most promising vaccine candidate would not be ready for clinical trials for 6–9 months. The virus spreads through close contact with bodily fluids of sick or deceased patients; healthcare workers and family members are at highest risk. Mortality is likely around 30% or higher, though precise figures are uncertain due to limited experience. Two prior Bundibugyo outbreaks occurred in the same Congo River basin region, and the virus was first identified in 2007 by CDC's Special Pathogens Branch led by Dr Tom Ksiazek. Public health priorities include early case finding, isolation, contact tracing, PPE for workers, safe burial practices, and supportive care (IV/oral fluids) to reduce mortality.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in Central Africa, centered in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ituri province near the Uganda border, with border screening at the Grande Barrier crossing between Congo and Rwanda in Goma on May 18, 2026. The WHO has declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. Reported figures exceed 300 suspected cases and at least 137 deaths, mainly in DRC and adjacent Uganda. The Bundibugyo strain is a rare Ebola variant with an estimated 25–50% case fatality; no approved vaccines or treatments exist. Transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids; airborne spread is not implicated. Incubation is 2–21 days; symptoms include fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, and sometimes hemorrhage. A U.S. citizen exposed in Congo is treated in Berlin; six more high‑risk evacuees were identified. The CDC imposes 30‑day entry restrictions for travelers from DRC, South Sudan, and Uganda; MSF is expanding operations in Bunia.
